heroLead: Beech Bottom runs along a thin strip of the Ohio River in Brooke County, one of the narrowest counties in West Virginia, where mineral tracts tend to be long, riverfront-oriented slivers rather than square farm parcels.
intro: Brooke County's geography shaped how land got divided here: narrow strips running back from the river toward the hills meant fewer, longer tracts, but the mineral rights under them have split among heirs just as thoroughly as anywhere else in the Northern Panhandle. Beech Bottom sits in the deeper part of the play, where Utica and Point Pleasant leasing has picked up alongside older shallow production.
We buy mineral and royalty interests around Beech Bottom directly, working from the actual deed and lease record for your specific tract rather than a general sense of what the neighborhood pays.

sections.heading: Deep Utica leasing over legacy shallow wells
paragraphs: The Northern Panhandle sits over some of the deepest, most productive Utica and Point Pleasant rock in the play, and Brooke County has seen real leasing activity from operators targeting those zones. It's common for a Beech Bottom tract to carry both a decades-old shallow gas lease and a newer deep-rights lease, layered on the same acreage with different terms.

sections.heading: Industrial and riverfront tract history
paragraphs: Beech Bottom's proximity to river industry means some tracts here were split between surface sales to industrial users and mineral reservations kept by the original family. That pattern produces mineral owners who no longer live anywhere near the property and may not track lease activity closely.

sections.heading: Reading the actual lease before we price it
paragraphs: Whether your tract is under an old flat-rate lease, a modern deep-rights lease, or both, we pull the recorded instrument at the Brooke County Courthouse in Wellsburg before naming a number, so the offer reflects your real terms and unit position.

faqs.question: Does my Beech Bottom tract have both shallow and deep leases?
faqs.answer: It's possible. Many Northern Panhandle tracts carry a legacy shallow-well lease alongside a separate modern lease covering Utica or Point Pleasant rights.

faqs.question: How do you value a riverfront mineral tract differently?
faqs.answer: Value comes from lease terms, unit production, and depth of rights owned, not the surface geography, though narrow historic tracts can complicate title tracing.

faqs.question: What if my family sold the surface but kept the minerals decades ago?
faqs.answer: That's a common pattern here. We trace the severance deed to confirm what was reserved and to whom before making an offer.
